title: OKUP study: 91% of cheated migrant workers had no written contract before leaving
excerpt: A study of 85 complaints to BMET's arbitration system found all male workers paid above the official fee. Malaysia-bound workers paid 5.8 times the fixed rate.
content:
Nine in ten migrant workers who complained of being cheated abroad had not received a written employment contract before leaving Bangladesh, a study by the migrant rights organisation Ovibashi Karmi Unnayan Program (OKUP) found. It was presented at a Dhaka hotel on Wednesday (25 November), The Daily Star reported.

The study, "Justice by Procedure? A Legal and Institutional Audit of BMET Arbitration for Migrant Workers", followed the complaints of 50 men and 35 women between November 2024 and June 2026 and included 20 in-depth case studies. It looked at how the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) handles workers' complaints through arbitration.

All 50 men said they had paid recruitment fees above the government-fixed rate. Malaysia-bound workers paid 5.8 times the fixed fee, those going to the UAE and Jordan 4.2 times, Saudi Arabia 2.8 times and Singapore 2.7 times. Half of the men got no job on arrival, and 78% reported job deception. All 35 women reported wage exploitation; 97% said they faced mental abuse, 89% confinement or isolation and 77% physical abuse. Fifteen per cent of all respondents had pre-departure orientation certificates without attending the training.

Shakirul Islam, OKUP chairperson and lead researcher, said recruitment costs equalled nearly 15 months of a worker's overseas earnings. He asked how BMET issued emigration clearance without making sure workers had contracts and training, when cheated workers are later asked to show those same contracts to back their complaints. Saadia Aleem, head of protection at IOM Bangladesh, said: "This is not a contract dispute. This is trafficking. This is crime." She said mediation may secure compensation but cannot replace criminal investigation and prosecution.

BMET Director (Employment) Md Masud Rana challenged several findings. He said visas for female domestic workers going to Saudi Arabia cannot be processed without a signed contract uploaded to the recruitment platform, that workers may not have understood the terms used, and that biometric attendance is required for pre-departure training. He asked the researchers to share details so BMET could look into them.

The sample is small and made up of workers who had complained, so it does not show how common these problems are among all migrants.

Why it matters

Migrant welfare NGOs and legal aid groups often guide workers through BMET arbitration. The study suggests the process treats serious abuse as a contract dispute and depends on documents many workers never received. It adds to calls to treat deception and forced labour as trafficking under the 2012 anti-trafficking law.

What to watch

  • BMET's response to the specific cases OKUP shares.
  • Enforcement of written contracts and real pre-departure training before emigration clearance.
  • Changes to recruitment fee rules for Malaysia, where costs were highest.

Sources
